lessons.title: Understand what Veo in Gemini can (and can't) do today, and generate your first clip
lessons.summary: Get a grounded picture of what Veo 3.1, accessed through the Gemini app, can reliably do in 2026, then generate one usable clip to calibrate your expectations.
lessons.goal: Generate one short Veo clip in the Gemini app, after first learning the realistic capabilities and limits of AI video generation today.
lessons.whyItMatters: AI video is now genuinely useful for social content, product marketing and quick previz, and Veo 3.1 — accessed through the Gemini app — is the widely rated all-round leader: strongest prompt adherence, native synchronized audio, and reliable image-to-video. (Landscape note: other tools like Runway, Kling and Pika exist for specific needs — heavier manual control, natural human motion, or ultra-cheap social experiments — and OpenAI's Sora consumer app shut down entirely in April 2026, a reminder that even a frontier lab's flagship video product can disappear. This course teaches transferable prompting skills using Veo in Gemini as the primary tool.) Knowing what Veo actually does well today, and where it still struggles, is what separates realistic expectations from wasted Google AI Pro or Ultra credits.
steps: Understand Veo 3.1's access: it lives inside the Gemini app under a Google AI Pro (~$19.99/mo) or Ultra plan; the Gemini free tier doesn't include meaningful Veo access, so budget for at least the Pro plan before you start generating.

Understand what Veo reliably does today: short clips (typically 5-8 seconds per generation, extendable with scene extension), animating a still photo into motion (image-to-video, including a frame you designed with Nano Banana), camera moves, style transfer, and native synchronized audio and dialogue generated together with the video, not bolted on afterward.

Understand current limits: consistency across many separate shots still needs deliberate continuity technique, exact on-screen text and logos render unreliably, hands and complex physics can glitch, and each generation is one draw from a random process — expect to regenerate rather than get a perfect first result.
Open the Gemini app (web or mobile) and confirm your plan includes Veo generation before you start.
Write one simple prompt describing a single shot: subject, one clear action, setting, one camera move, one simple sound cue, and style — not a whole story.
Generate the clip and watch it fully at least twice, comparing what you asked for — including the audio — against what you actually got.
Write down which specific things matched your prompt and which didn't — this is how you build calibrated intuition for Veo's particular strengths and quirks.
lessons.prompt: A steaming cup of coffee sits on a wooden table by a rain-streaked window. Camera slowly pushes in. Soft morning light, shallow depth of field, gentle steam rising. Ambient sound: quiet rain against the glass, faint kitchen ambience. Cinematic, photorealistic. 5 seconds.
lessons.explanation: This prompt works because it names one subject, one continuous camera move, one lighting condition, one simple sound cue, and one style in a single sentence — nothing sequential, nothing that requires Veo to guess at timing or invent an audio track from scratch. It's deliberately simple because your first clip should test the tool's baseline behavior, not your prompting skill.
lessons.example:
Input: the coffee-cup prompt above.

Typical output: a 5-6 second photorealistic clip with a slow push-in on the cup, visible steam, soft window light, and a quiet rain-and-kitchen ambience synced to the picture — usually close to the brief, though the exact steam pattern, push-in speed, or how prominent the rain sound is will vary between attempts.
lessons.exercise: In the Gemini app, write a simple motion-first prompt (including a sound cue) for something relevant to your own work — a product, a scene, a mood you want to test — and generate one clip. Watch it fully at least twice.
lessons.expectedResult: You have one generated clip and can name at least two things Veo got right and one or two things that differed from your prompt, including whether the audio matched what you described.
commonMistakes: Expecting a single prompt to produce a multi-shot story or a finished ad — one generation is one shot, not a sequence.
Assuming Veo renders exact on-screen text or logos reliably — treat that as an editing-stage task, not a generation-stage one.
Leaving the sound cue out of your prompt and being surprised Veo generated an audio track anyway — it always generates audio, so describe what you want it to be.
Judging Veo from a single disappointing generation instead of trying a few variations before forming an opinion.
lessons.proTip: Keep a running note of prompt-to-actual-output pairs, including whether the audio matched what you described — it's the fastest way to build your own mental model of exactly what Veo does well on your Gemini plan and where it struggles.

lessons.title: Write motion-first Veo prompts that actually control the shot
lessons.summary: Learn the six-part anatomy of an effective Veo prompt — subject, action, camera, setting/lighting, style, and sound — so your clips stop looking like random guesses.
lessons.goal: Write and generate three variations of a prompt for the same scene, changing one variable at a time — camera move, then style — to learn what each one actually controls in Veo.
lessons.whyItMatters: The biggest shift from image prompting to video prompting is describing motion — and, in Veo's case, sound — not just a picture. A prompt that only describes what a frame looks like leaves Veo to guess how it moves and what it sounds like, and that guess is where most disappointing clips come from. Prompt discipline is the single highest-leverage skill in this course, and it's what makes the Gemini app's Veo integration worth learning properly rather than clicking generate and hoping.
steps: Learn the six-part anatomy: Subject (who or what), Action (one clear continuous motion), Camera (static, push in, pan, orbit, handheld, drone), Setting/lighting (where, time of day, light quality), Style (photorealistic, cinematic, animated, a specific film look), and Sound (ambient noise, dialogue, a music cue) — Veo generates audio natively, so leaving sound unstated is still a choice, just an unintentional one.
Write the action as one continuous motion, not a sequence of events — a 5-8 second clip cannot show 'she stands up, walks to the door, opens it' as three distinct beats.
Name the camera move explicitly. Veo defaults to something, often a static shot or a slow generic push, if you leave it unstated — being explicit is how you take control.
Add pacing language (slow and gentle versus quick and dynamic), since it changes how much visibly happens within the clip's short duration.
Keep style and lighting descriptors specific but few — two or three well-chosen words beat a long list, which tends to blend into a muddier, less controlled look.
Describe sound deliberately, even a simple phrase like 'quiet ambient room tone' — Veo generates audio either way, so an unstated sound cue is just another detail left to chance.
Generate a baseline clip, then regenerate changing only the camera move, then regenerate again changing only the style — compare all three to isolate what each variable actually controls.
Note which variable produced the biggest visible (or audible) difference — that becomes your instinct for which 'knob' matters most going forward.
lessons.prompt:
BASELINE: A cyclist rides down a coastal road at sunset. Camera tracks alongside at the cyclist's speed, staying level. Golden hour light, warm tones, cinematic, realistic. Ambient sound: wind, distant waves, tires humming on pavement. 5 seconds.

VARIANT A (camera only): same subject, action and sound as the baseline, but the camera pulls back and up into a slow aerial drone shot revealing the coastline.

VARIANT B (style only): same subject, action, camera and sound as the baseline, but the style shifts to gritty 16mm film grain, desaturated color, documentary look.
lessons.explanation: Running one baseline plus two single-variable variants isolates cause and effect — you learn exactly what changing 'camera' versus 'style' does in Veo instead of guessing from one messy attempt that changed everything at once. Holding the action and sound line identical across all three also reinforces the habit of describing one continuous motion and one deliberate audio cue, rather than a sequence of events or an afterthought.
lessons.example:
Input: the baseline plus two variants above.

Output: three clips of the same cyclist scene — a level tracking shot, then a rising aerial reveal of the same action, then the same tracking shot rendered in a grainier documentary look — all carrying the same wind-and-waves ambience, making it easy to see exactly what each variable changed.
lessons.exercise: Pick a scene relevant to your own work, write a baseline prompt plus a camera-only variant and a style-only variant, and generate all three in the Gemini app.
lessons.expectedResult: Three clips of the same scene where you can point to exactly what changed between them and confirm Veo followed your instruction for that one variable.
commonMistakes: Packing multiple sequential actions into one prompt instead of one continuous motion.
Leaving camera movement unspecified, then being surprised by generic default motion.
Overloading style descriptors so Veo blends several unrelated aesthetics into a muddy result.
Treating a single generation as final instead of understanding it as one draw from a random process — regenerate before rewriting the whole prompt.
lessons.proTip: If a clip has a recurring glitch, describe what to avoid directly in the prompt sentence itself — for example 'hands stay out of frame' or 'no on-screen text' — rather than only describing what you want. The Gemini app doesn't have a separate negative-prompt field, so folding exclusions into the main prompt is often the most reliable lever you have.

lessons.title: Plan shots with ChatGPT and turn an idea into a storyboard of Veo prompts
lessons.summary: Use ChatGPT to draft a shot list from a concept, then write one tightly scoped Veo prompt per shot with a shared continuity block so a multi-clip sequence actually holds together.
lessons.goal: Produce a written shot list of 4-6 shots with one complete Veo prompt per shot, all sharing an explicit continuity block, so the sequence reads as one coherent piece rather than disconnected clips.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A short concept for a 15-30 second piece — a product teaser, a mood piece, a brand intro — and access to ChatGPT and the Gemini app.
lessons.whyItMatters: Any real 20-30 second piece needs multiple clips stitched together, and continuity — the same subject appearance, the same setting, a consistent visual style — is the single biggest failure point when people generate shots independently without planning. Using ChatGPT to turn a one-sentence idea into a structured shot list before you touch Veo separates planning from generation, so you enter the Gemini app already knowing the beats instead of improvising shot by shot.
steps: Write the concept and outcome in one sentence — what the finished piece is for and where it will run.

Paste that sentence into ChatGPT and ask it to break the concept into a shot list of 4-6 shots, each covering one clear beat (an opening establishing shot, a subject or product reveal, a detail or action shot, a closing shot), with a rough duration per shot.

Treat ChatGPT's shot list as a starting point, not a finished prompt — it drafts the beats, but you still write each shot as a proper motion-first Veo prompt yourself, since a general chat model doesn't know Veo's prompt conventions the way this course does.

Write a fixed continuity block: a reusable phrase describing the subject's exact appearance, the environment, and the visual style, and paste that same block into every shot's prompt so the description doesn't drift from shot to shot.
For each shot, write one motion-first Veo prompt combining the continuity block with that shot's specific action, camera move, and a sound cue.
Check that every prompt uses the same wording for the same element — don't call it 'a red mug' in shot 1 and 'a ceramic cup' in shot 3.

Generate shots in order in the Gemini app, comparing each new shot's look against the previous one before moving on, and regenerate early if continuity is already drifting rather than waiting until the end.

Check Veo's own continuity tools — animating from a reference image as the first frame, or using scene extension to continue directly from a previous shot's last frame — these reduce drift more reliably than the text continuity block alone.
Do a rough mental (or quick editor) run-through of the sequence to sanity-check pacing before treating any shot as final.
lessons.promptLabel: Copyable prompt (shot-list request + continuity block + shot prompts)
lessons.prompt:
SHOT-LIST REQUEST (paste into ChatGPT first): I'm making a 20-second brand mood piece about a calm morning coffee ritual. Break it into 4-6 shots, each covering one clear beat (opening establishing shot, subject reveal, a detail or action shot, a closing shot). For each shot, give a one-line description and a rough duration in seconds.

CONTINUITY BLOCK (paste into every Veo shot prompt): A woman with short black hair wearing a cream linen shirt, in a sunlit minimalist kitchen with white walls and wooden countertops. Style: clean, photorealistic, soft natural light, warm neutral tones.

SHOT 1 (establishing): [CONTINUITY BLOCK] Wide shot, she stands at the counter pouring coffee. Camera static, slight ambient movement only. Ambient sound: quiet kitchen, gentle pour. 5 seconds.

SHOT 2 (detail): [CONTINUITY BLOCK] Close-up on her hands wrapping around the warm mug. Camera slow push in. Ambient sound: soft room tone. 4 seconds.

SHOT 3 (reveal): [CONTINUITY BLOCK] Medium shot, she looks up and smiles toward the window light. Camera holds, then a gentle slow pan right. Ambient sound: soft room tone, faint birdsong outside. 5 seconds.
lessons.explanation: Asking ChatGPT for the shot list first, then rewriting each beat as a proper Veo prompt, separates the creative-planning step from the generation step, which is where most people skip straight to prompting and lose the thread of the whole piece. Pasting an identical continuity block into every shot, and reusing the exact same wording for recurring elements, is what stops Veo from quietly re-imagining the subject or setting between generations.
lessons.example:
Input: a concept for a 20-second morning-coffee brand mood piece, broken into 4 shots by ChatGPT, then rewritten as Veo prompts sharing the continuity block above.

Output: 4 generated clips with a consistent subject and kitchen across all of them; a lighting mismatch caught in shot 3 during review gets regenerated immediately rather than discovered only after all 4 shots were generated.
lessons.exercise: Ask ChatGPT to draft a 4-6 shot list for a real concept from your own work, build a continuity block, rewrite at least 2 shots as Veo prompts, and generate them in the Gemini app to compare continuity between them.
lessons.expectedResult: A written shot list with one Veo prompt per shot sharing a consistent continuity block, and at least 2 shots generated and visually compared for continuity.
commonMistakes: Pasting ChatGPT's shot-list output straight into Veo as-is instead of rewriting each beat into a proper motion-first prompt with camera, sound and continuity details.
Writing each shot's prompt independently without a shared continuity block, causing the subject or setting to drift between shots.
Describing the same element with different wording across shots, which reads to Veo as a different element.
Generating the whole shot list before reviewing any of it, so drift compounds before you catch it.
lessons.proTip: Keep your ChatGPT shot list, continuity block, and final Veo prompts together in one running notes file per project — reuse it if you need to regenerate weeks later for a revision, since rewriting the description from memory almost never produces the same look twice.

lessons.title: Create product and promo clips for social media with Veo image-to-video
lessons.summary: Animate a real product photo into a short vertical social clip with a hook-first structure, using Veo's image-to-video so the product's appearance stays accurate.
lessons.goal: Produce one vertical (9:16) product or promo clip, 6-15 seconds long, using Veo image-to-video from a real product photo, structured around a hook in the first 1-2 seconds.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A product photo — your own or a stock/mockup image — and the platform format you're targeting, typically 9:16 for Reels, TikTok, or Shorts.
lessons.whyItMatters: Most real AI video demand from marketers and creators is short, social-first product content, and image-to-video — animating your own real product photo in Veo rather than describing the product from scratch — reliably keeps packaging, logo, and color accurate. That matters because text-to-video's imprecise rendering of exact text and logos is a known limitation of every current video generator; feeding in a real photo sidesteps it entirely.
steps: Choose the platform and aspect ratio — 9:16 vertical for Reels, TikTok, and Shorts is typical — and a clip length target; 6-15 seconds in a single clip is easiest for a first attempt.

Start from a real photo of the actual product, not a text-only description, and use Veo's image-to-video feature in the Gemini app so packaging, logo, and color stay accurate instead of being reinvented by the model.
If you don't have a clean product photo, generate one first with Nano Banana (Gemini's image tool) and use that as your first frame instead — the same image-to-video discipline still applies.

Write the animation prompt describing only the motion to add to that still image — a camera move and/or a small product action, such as a slow rotation or light catching the surface — not the product's appearance, since the photo already defines that.

Add a short sound cue matching the mood, or explicitly say 'no music, quiet ambient room tone only' if you want a clean, near-silent track — Veo generates audio either way, so state your intent rather than leaving it to chance.

Structure pacing around a hook: something visually attention-grabbing should happen in the first 1-2 seconds, with motion starting immediately rather than holding on a static frame, since social platforms lose viewers fast.

Generate the clip and check the product itself for fidelity issues — a warped logo, a shifted color, or invented text is the most common social product-clip failure, and usually means cropping the source photo tighter or simplifying the animation prompt.
Export in the platform's native resolution and aspect ratio, and plan to add text overlay and captions in a simple editor afterward rather than expecting exact on-screen text from Veo itself.
lessons.prompt: Animate this product photo: the perfume bottle rotates slowly a quarter turn, catching soft studio light across the glass. Camera holds static, with a slight slow zoom in over the full clip. Background stays clean and unchanged. Ambient sound: quiet studio room tone only, no music. 6 seconds, no added text, no logo changes.
lessons.explanation: The prompt describes only motion and sound because the source photo already defines the product's appearance — asking Veo to also describe the product invites it to reinvent details like label text. The explicit 'no text, no logo changes' guardrail directly targets the most common product-fidelity failure, and naming the sound intent ('quiet room tone only, no music') keeps Veo's native audio generation from adding an unwanted soundtrack.
lessons.example:
Input: a photo of a skincare bottle plus the prompt above, adapted to that product.

Output: a 6-second vertical clip with the bottle rotating and light catching it, the product's appearance matching the source photo, and a quiet room-tone audio track. Contrast: writing a text-only prompt describing the same bottle from scratch risks Veo changing the label text or bottle shape entirely.
lessons.exercise: Use your own product photo, or a stock one, in the Gemini app's image-to-video feature. Write a motion-and-sound-only prompt following the guardrails above and generate a 9:16 clip.
lessons.expectedResult: A vertical product clip where the product's appearance matches the source photo, with no invented text, logo, or color changes, a deliberate (not accidental) audio track, and camera or product motion that creates a hook within the first 1-2 seconds.
commonMistakes: Describing the product's full appearance in a text-to-video prompt instead of animating a real photo, inviting Veo to reinvent details like label text.
Opening on a slow, static hold instead of motion that hooks attention before the 2-second mark.
Leaving the sound cue unstated and getting a generic or mismatched music track instead of the clean, quiet audio the piece actually needs.
Expecting Veo to render final on-screen marketing text reliably instead of adding it during editing.
lessons.proTip: Generate 2-3 short variants of the same product animation, such as different camera moves, in one session — since Veo has no meaningful free tier, spend your Google AI Pro or Ultra credits deliberately on a small A/B set rather than trying to perfect a single generation through many retries.

lessons.title: Iterate on Veo output: extend, retime, and fix problem clips
lessons.summary: Match the right technique — scene extension, a targeted fix, or a full regenerate — to a specific clip problem, and stretch short clips into usable longer sequences.
lessons.goal: Take one existing Veo-generated clip with a specific flaw or a too-short duration, and produce an improved or extended version using Veo's iteration features in the Gemini app.
lessons.whyItMatters: First-generation output is rarely final, and a budget-conscious workflow means iterating cheaply on a flawed clip instead of either regenerating from scratch every time or shipping a flaw you noticed but didn't fix. Single Veo generations also cap around 5-8 seconds, so scene extension is how you reach a usable social or promo length of 15-30 seconds without visibly stitching together mismatched separate clips.
steps: Identify which category of problem you actually have: too short (needs extension), a wrong local detail such as a warped hand or a weird object, wrong pacing or timing, a mismatched audio track, or a fundamentally wrong overall take.

For 'too short,' use Veo's scene extension feature in the Gemini app, which continues from the clip's final frame rather than generating a new unrelated clip, preserving both visual and audio continuity automatically.

Write extension prompts describing only what happens next, referencing that it continues directly from the current motion, framing and sound — don't re-describe the whole scene, which risks Veo treating it as a new, disconnected shot.

For a wrong local detail, such as a glitchy hand or a distorted object, regenerate with a small, targeted addition naming the exact fix, such as 'keep hands out of frame,' rather than rewriting the entire prompt, since the rest of it was already working.

For a mismatched audio track — music that clashes with the mood, or dialogue that wasn't asked for — regenerate with a more explicit sound line, such as 'ambient room tone only, no music, no dialogue,' since vague sound cues are the most common cause of an unwanted track.

For pacing problems, where motion happens too fast or too slow for the clip length, adjust pacing language explicitly, such as adding 'slow, gentle' or 'quick, energetic,' and regenerate — duration and pacing wording interact, so retest after any change.

For a take that's fundamentally wrong in composition, mood, or subject placement, don't try to patch it — regenerate from a revised prompt, since patching a fundamentally wrong take usually costs more attempts than starting over.
Track how many regenerations a given shot needed and which specific fix worked — this becomes your personal troubleshooting reference for Veo's quirks.
Once you have a final clip or an extended sequence, watch it fully at real speed to confirm the fix didn't introduce a new visual or audio problem elsewhere.
lessons.prompt:
EXTEND (continuing directly from the last frame, same subject, setting, style and sound — do not restart or redescribe the scene): the cyclist continues along the coastal road as it curves right, camera keeps tracking alongside at the same speed and height, sunset light now slightly lower and warmer, same wind-and-waves ambience continuing. 4 more seconds.

TARGETED FIX (regenerate the previous shot with one added constraint, everything else unchanged): same prompt as before, but keep both of the cyclist's hands gripping the handlebars throughout, no additional camera movement beyond the original lateral track.
lessons.explanation: Extension prompts deliberately avoid redescribing the scene because that re-description is exactly what causes Veo to treat it as a new shot instead of a continuation, and naming the sound as continuing too keeps the audio from resetting or drifting at the join. Targeted-fix prompts change as little as possible on top of a prompt that was already mostly working, which preserves everything that was correct while addressing only the specific flaw — a full regenerate is reserved for when the whole take is wrong, not used as the default response to any problem.
lessons.example:
Input: a good 5-second clip with a glitchy hand at second 3.

Output: a targeted-fix prompt keeps the rest of the description identical and adds a hand constraint, producing a clean version without needing to rewrite the whole scene from scratch.
lessons.exercise: Take a clip from an earlier lesson, or generate a quick new one, identify one specific flaw or its short duration, and apply the matching technique — extension, targeted fix, or full regenerate — in the Gemini app.
lessons.expectedResult: An improved or extended clip, plus a short note on which iteration technique you used and why it matched the specific problem.
commonMistakes: Rewriting an entire prompt from scratch to fix one small flaw, which changes parts of the shot that were already working.
Re-describing the whole scene in an extension prompt instead of continuing from the last frame, which often produces a visibly disconnected new shot with a jarring audio jump.
Endlessly regenerating a fundamentally wrong take hoping a small tweak fixes it, instead of recognizing when to start over.
Not watching the full extended or fixed clip at real speed before calling it final, missing a new visual or audio problem the fix introduced.
lessons.proTip: Save the exact prompt text for every generation you keep — when you need a small fix later, you edit that saved prompt directly rather than trying to reconstruct it, sound cue included, from memory.

lessons.title: Build a realistic production workflow: Veo clips plus simple editing, start to finish
lessons.summary: Combine multiple Veo-generated clips with basic editing — cuts, text overlay, captions, final audio mix — into one finished, publishable short video using a repeatable process.
lessons.goal: Produce one finished, exportable short video (15-40 seconds) that combines 3 or more Veo-generated clips with cuts, text overlay or captions, and a clean audio mix, ready to publish.
lessons.beforeYouStart: The shot list and prompts from an earlier lesson, or a new short concept; access to the Gemini app for Veo generation; and a basic video editor with a timeline and text/audio tracks — a phone editor such as CapCut, or a desktop tool such as Premiere, DaVinci Resolve, or Descript.
lessons.whyItMatters: A real production workflow, not just individual clips, is what actually ships — clients and audiences see the finished edited piece, not the raw generations. Veo generates footage and audio; it doesn't finish a piece of content. Combining generation with a simple, repeatable edit pass is what turns a folder of clips into a piece of content, and this end-to-end process is what makes everything else in this course usable at work, rather than a series of one-off demos.
steps: Finalize your shot list and generate all clips first, using the ChatGPT-assisted storyboard and continuity techniques from earlier lessons, collecting the best take of each shot in one project folder before opening an editor.

If you need more generation-time control than the Gemini app's chat interface offers — a dedicated storyboard view, finer scene-by-scene editing — Google's Flow tool runs the same Veo 3.1 model with a purpose-built filmmaking interface; it's worth trying once you're comfortable with the basics.

Import all clips into your editor's timeline in shot order and do a rough cut first — trim each clip to its usable portion, often the best 2-4 seconds of a 5-8 second generation, before worrying about polish.

Check pacing on the rough cut by watching it straight through once: Veo clips often run slightly long or have a weak first or last frame, so trim heads and tails aggressively for social-length content.

Review the audio Veo already generated for each clip: since Veo produces synchronized sound natively, you often need less added music than you'd expect — keep what works, mute or replace what doesn't, and duck anything under dialogue or voiceover.

Add text directly in the editor: captions if there's dialogue or voiceover, and any on-screen marketing text such as product name, price, or CTA, since editors render exact text reliably and Veo doesn't.

Apply a consistent color or look across clips if generations from different sessions don't quite match — a simple LUT, filter, or a manual match of exposure and warmth closes small mismatches between shots.
Add a clear opening hook in the first 1-2 seconds and a closing CTA frame appropriate to the platform, since these are the two moments viewers actually remember.
Export at the platform's required spec — resolution, aspect ratio, format — and do one final full watch-through on the actual target device, usually a phone, before publishing.
Save the project file, shot list, and prompts together in one folder — this becomes your reusable template for the next piece instead of rebuilding the whole workflow from scratch.
lessons.prompt:
I've combined [NUMBER] Veo-generated clips into a [LENGTH]-second video for [PLATFORM]. Here's my rough edit description: [DESCRIBE YOUR CUT ORDER, MUSIC CHOICE, TEXT OVERLAYS, AND ANY COLOR MATCHING YOU DID].

Act as a critical editor reviewing this before I publish. Tell me:
1. Whether the described pacing sounds right for [PLATFORM]'s typical attention span — call out anything that sounds too slow to open or too long overall.
2. Whether the hook (first 1-2 seconds) and the closing CTA are clearly described, or missing.
3. One thing in this description that sounds like it could still read as "obviously AI" rather than produced content, and a specific fix.
Base your answer only on what I've described — don't assume details I haven't given you.
lessons.explanation: This is a text-based sanity-check prompt for Claude, not a video generation prompt — it's a final review step before publishing. Restricting the AI to only what you've described, rather than letting it assume unstated details, produces a grounded critique instead of generic advice, and a fresh set of 'eyes' reliably catches pacing and hook issues that a creator too close to their own footage tends to miss.
lessons.example:
Input: a description of a 25-second Reel with 4 clips, Veo's native audio kept as-is, no captions, and a static opening hold.

Output: flags the weak opening — a static clip for the first 2 seconds — as the biggest risk for the platform, confirms the CTA frame is present, and suggests trimming the opening clip's static portion before publishing.
lessons.exercise: Build one complete short video end to end: generate or reuse 3 or more Veo clips, edit them together with text, captions and a hook/CTA structure, then paste the review prompt above into Claude with your own description before exporting and publishing.
lessons.expectedResult: One finished, exported video combining 3 or more Veo clips with cuts, text or captions, a clean audio mix, a clear hook and CTA, reviewed against the checklist prompt before publishing.
commonMistakes: Treating raw Veo clip output as the finished product and skipping editing entirely, which usually reads as unpolished even when individual clips look great.
Using each clip's full duration instead of trimming to its best portion, leaving weak opening or closing frames in the final cut.
Relying on Veo for on-screen marketing text or captions instead of adding them in the editor, where they render reliably.
Not testing the final export on the actual target device or app before publishing, missing crop or caption-safe-zone issues specific to that platform.
lessons.proTip: Build a lightweight personal template — default sound-cue phrasing, caption style, intro/outro frame, export presets — once you've made 2-3 of these pieces. The editing pass, not the generation pass, is where most of the repeatable time savings show up after your first few projects.
